title: Systematic characterization of myoclonus-dystonia syndrome with manifestation in childhood and adolescence
summary:
The myoclonus-dystonia syndrome is a rare neurological disorder that can manifest already in early childhood and is often associated with mutations in the SGCE gene. It is characterized by involuntary, brief muscle jerks (myoclonus) and sustained or intermittent muscle contractions (dystonias), as well as possible psychiatric comorbidities that can significantly affect the quality of life of those affected. The severity of the disorder varies greatly. So far, there is only limited data on disease progression and treatment response in childhood and adolescence. As part of the ESNEK survey (Survey for Rare Neurological Disorders in Childhood), we are managing a registry database through which we aim to collect data on these patients across Germany.
The aim of the study is the systematic characterization of pediatric patients with myoclonus-dystonia syndrome, including the various gene variants, the respective course of the disease, achieved therapy effects, and possible comorbidities. In the long term, the data basis is intended to contribute to the development of evidence-based treatment strategies and to improve the care of affected patients. To collect the data, standardized clinical examinations are conducted and questionnaires are used.

interventions.name: In the initial contact, patients with myoclonus dystonia syndrome provide extensive anamnestic and clinical information about their current status and the course since the onset of the disease. criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
• Myoclonus-dystonia syndrome
• Proven pathogenic or suspected pathogenic mutation in SGCE or
• Clinical diagnosis of myoclonus-dystonia syndrome without genetic evidence
• Written consent before the start of data collection, depending on age and psycho-intellectual development signed by patients, parents, or legal guardians
• Patient age between 6 months and 25 years.
Exclusion criteria:
• Missing consent form
• Secondary myoclonus or secondary dystonia as a result of structural brain damage or a progressive neurodegenerative disease
